Beyond Task-Agnostic: Task-Aware Grouping for Communication-Efficient Multi-Task MoE Inference

Zhiyao Xu Affiliation: Tsinghua Shenzhen International Graduate School, Shenzhen, China Email: xu-zy25@mails.tsinghua.edu.cn    Aoxue Liu Affiliation: Tsinghua Shenzhen International Graduate School, Shenzhen, China Email: lax25@mails.tsinghua.edu.cn    Zhanjie Ding Affiliation: Tsinghua Shenzhen International Graduate School, Shenzhen, China Email: dingzj25@mails.tsinghua.edu.cn    Dan Zhao11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: Pengcheng Laboratory, Shenzhen, China Email: zhaod01@pcl.ac.cn    Yong Jiang11footnotemark: 1 ††thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation: Tsinghua Shenzhen International Graduate School, Shenzhen, China Affiliation: Pengcheng Laboratory, Shenzhen, China Email: liq@pcl.ac.cn    Qing Li Affiliation: Pengcheng Laboratory, Shenzhen, China Email: jiangy@sz.tsinghua.edu.cn
Abstract

Sparsely activated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale capacity via conditional computation, but distributed inference suffers from cross-GPU expert communication and routing-induced load imbalance. Existing placement methods reduce this cost by co-locating frequently co-activated experts; however, they derive a single deployment plan from globally aggregated routing traces, thereby averaging away the heterogeneous, task-specific co-activation patterns that actually drive communication in multi-task serving. We observe that expert co-activation is strongly task-conditioned: pairs tightly coupled in one task family are often uncorrelated in another, so effective deployment should group experts by task-aware co-activation rather than by a task-agnostic average. Based on this insight, we propose Task-Aware Coactivation Grouping (TACG), a deployment-time framework that uses family-specific dispatch and co-activation traces to derive per-expert task-family preferences, reweights the co-activation graph so that intra-family locality dominates grouping, and assigns each expert to a primary GPU under exact capacity constraints. To keep the static placement robust under online workload skew, we further introduce Generic Expert Shared Replication (GESR), a lightweight companion that identifies generic experts with consistently central co-activation profiles, replicates them across a small set of secondary GPUs, and applies locality- and load-aware selection at serving time. Experiments on three representative open-source MoE models demonstrate that our framework reduces the average communication cost by 31.39% over the baseline, while preserving an average Jain fairness index of 0.9975. This advantage persists even under severe distribution shifts in the inference data, consistently outperforming strong baselines.

1 Introduction

By leveraging conditional computation, MoE can significantly increase model capacity without a proportional increase in floating-point operations, and has therefore been widely adopted in all kinds of models [1, 2, 3]. Despite this advantage, MoE models typically impose substantially higher memory demands than their dense counterparts, often exceeding the capacity of a single accelerator. Consequently, large-scale MoE inference is commonly deployed using a combination of expert parallelism and data parallelism [2, 4, 5]. In this setting, experts in each MoE layer are distributed across multiple GPUs and coordinated through All-to-All communication. Although this distributed design enables scalable deployment, it also introduces two key system challenges: excessive communication overhead and severe load imbalance. [6, 7] show that the all-to-all communication overhead generated by the expert distribution accounts for 30%-50% of the overall reasoning time overhead of MoE.

Existing MoE serving optimizations mitigate these costs from several complementary directions, including more efficient sparse kernels, improved All-to-All scheduling, expert placement, and dynamic replication [8, 9, 10, 11, 12]. Among them, expert placement is particularly attractive because it can reduce communication without altering the model architecture: if experts that are frequently co-activated are placed on the same GPU, each token contacts fewer remote devices during inference.

However, most existing strategies [13, 14, 15] estimate expert affinity from globally aggregated routing traces and then construct a single deployment plan shared by all incoming requests. Such a task-agnostic view is natural for homogeneous workloads, but it is increasingly misaligned with modern shared inference services that interleave multiple task (code, math, query, complex reasoning, etc.) requests. Averaging heterogeneous coactivation patterns into one graph collapses task-specific expert groups and leaves a substantial amount of communication locality unexploited, making this kind of grouping difficult to be universal.

Our key insight is that expert coactivation is strongly task-conditioned. As shown in Figure 1, two experts that are tightly coupled on one task family are often only weakly related on another, or even competing for capacity. This observation motivates us to shift the unit of coactivation analysis from the workload to task awareness. At the same time, once the actual reasoning data is shifted in distribution after deployment, the prior grouping without task awareness will not work properly because different task types often activate different expert collaboration patterns.

So we propose Task-Aware Coactivation Grouping (TACG), a deployment-time framework that converts task-conditioned coactivation into a capacity-feasible placement. It derives soft expert–family preferences from traces, constructs a task-modulated coactivation graph, making task structure an explicit driver of locality. To protect these locality gains against load skew caused by a few generic experts that become hotspots under workload shift, we pair TACG with a lightweight Generic Expert Shared Replication (GESR) module, which identifies such experts via coactivation centrality and cross-family consistency, assigns each a small set of secondary GPUs chosen from structurally compatible non-primary cards, and selects replicas at serving time using a load-aware rule with exponentially decayed load signals.

We evaluate the proposed framework on three representative MoE models. Compared with the baseline placement, our method reduces the average communication metric by 31.39% across models, consistently improving over strong placement strategies. Meanwhile, this reduction is obtained while maintaining competitive load balance: our average Jain index remains 0.9975 and the average maximum load violation is 0.0736. Ablation studies confirm that the task-aware coactivation signal drives most of the gain, with GESR keeping load balance under control.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We identify that expert coactivation in multi-task MoE serving is strongly task-conditioned, and argue that an effective expert placement should be driven by task-aware coactivation rather than a single globally averaged affinity graph.

  • •

    We propose Task-Aware Coactivation Grouping (TACG), a task-aware strategy that reweights the coactivation graph by expert-to-family preferences and produces a capacity-feasible placement that strictly generalizes task-agnostic grouping.

  • •

    We propose Generic Expert Shared Replication (GESR), a lightweight companion that selectively replicates cross-family generic experts and performs load-aware online guard.

  • •

    We demonstrate on three representative MoE models that the framework delivers consistent communication reduction while retaining strong load-balance metrics, with ablations isolating the contribution of task-aware coactivation as the dominant factor.

2 Related Work

2.1 MoE Distributed Architectures and Expert Placement

Sparse Mixture-of-Experts architectures increase model capacity by routing each token to a small subset of experts. GShard [2] and Switch Transformer [16] established the dominant sparse-routing paradigm for large-scale Transformers, while BASE Layers [17] and Expert Choice routing [18] improve utilization and training stability through globally balanced assignment and expert-driven token selection. DeepSeekMoE [19] strengthens expert specialization via fine-grained expert partitioning and shared experts. A more closely related line studies expert placement itself. ExFlow [12] exploits inter-layer expert affinity for placement; C2R [13] uses collaboration-constrained routing to encourage specialized expert groups and reduce redundant communication; MoETuner [14] formulates placement as an ILP that jointly considers communication, computation, and load balance; and Semantic Parallelism [6] further reduces cross-group communication by semantically aligning token inputs to each group. Despite these advances, existing methods usually derive a single global placement from aggregated affinity, collaboration, or routing-dependency statistics, and do not explicitly analyze experts’ task preferences.

2.2 Task-Aware MoE

Task-aware MoE methods show that expert utility is often strongly conditioned on the task being served. MMoE [20] and DSelect-k [21] introduce task-specific gating for multi-task learning, demonstrating that different tasks benefit from different expert mixtures. Beyond Distillation [22] further shows that task-level routing can extract smaller and more efficient deployable sub-networks than token-level routing alone. Related pruning and adaptation methods, including Task-Specific Expert Pruning [23], Task-Based MoE [24], and HMoRA [25], also reveal that task information can be injected into routing or expert selection at different granularities. [26] improves the performance of MoE models by strengthening the experts’ task preferences through post-training with expert specialization. Recent research [7] from Meta also points to the potential of task-specific grouping. However, these approaches mainly act during training, fine-tuning, adaptation, or pruning.

3 Method

3.1 Overview

As illustrated in Figure 2, our framework runs an offline pipeline followed by an online guard. Offline, we first split calibration traffic by task family and collect per-family usage and coactivation statistics at every layer; we then score each expert’s task-family preference and use it to reweight the coactivation graph into a task-modulated graph; finally, spectral clustering with a capacity-repair pass groups experts on this graph, producing one primary GPU per expert—these three steps form Task-Aware Coactivation Grouping (TACG). Online, Generic Expert Shared Replication (GESR) flags a small set of cross-family generic experts, attaches a few secondary GPUs to each, and at serving time picks one candidate per token via a locality- and load-aware rule, leaving the MoE router untouched.

3.2 Problem Setup

Consider an MoE model with LL MoE layers, EE experts per layer, and MM GPUs, where each GPU denotes the expert-parallel serving unit. The task set is partitioned into K=4K=4 families.

ℱ={code,query,math,complex_reasoning}.\mathcal{F}=\{\texttt{code},\texttt{query},\texttt{math},\texttt{complex\_reasoning}\}. (1)

For each family f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F}, we reserve a disjoint GPU set 𝒢f\mathcal{G}_{f} with ∪f𝒢f={1,…,M}\cup_{f}\mathcal{G}_{f}=\{1,\ldots,M\}. Let BfB_{f} be the number of experts nominally allocated to family ff, with ∑fBf=E\sum_{f}B_{f}=E, and let Cf,mC_{f,m} be the capacity of GPU m∈𝒢fm\in\mathcal{G}_{f}, with ∑m∈𝒢fCf,m=Bf\sum_{m\in\mathcal{G}_{f}}C_{f,m}=B_{f}. Given calibration routing traces grouped by task family, TACG outputs a primary placement gl,eprimaryg_{l,e}^{\mathrm{primary}} for every expert; GESR then attaches a sparse candidate set 𝒞l,e\mathcal{C}_{l,e} to a small subset of generic experts. The MoE router itself is unchanged; all decisions are made at deployment and serving time. Section 3.3 details TACG, and Section 3.4 details GESR.

3.3 Task-Aware Coactivation Grouping (TACG)

Scoring task-family preference.

We first quantify how strongly each expert serves each task family. For each layer ll and family ff, we compute two statistics from calibration traces: the usage vector ul(f)∈ℝEu_{l}^{(f)}\in\mathbb{R}^{E} (relative dispatch frequency of each expert) and the coactivation matrix Al(f)∈ℝE×EA_{l}^{(f)}\in\mathbb{R}^{E\times E} (frequency of expert pairs selected by the same token). To avoid simply highlighting globally popular experts, we score each expert by its relative advantage for one family against the other families:

Δ​ul,e(f)=ul,e(f)−1K−1​∑f′≠ful,e(f′),cl,e(f)=∑e′|Al(f)​(e,e′)|,\Delta u_{l,e}^{(f)}=u_{l,e}^{(f)}-\frac{1}{K-1}\sum_{f^{\prime}\neq f}u_{l,e}^{(f^{\prime})},\qquad c_{l,e}^{(f)}=\sum_{e^{\prime}}\left|A_{l}^{(f)}(e,e^{\prime})\right|, (2)
Δ​cl,e(f)=cl,e(f)−1K−1​∑f′≠fcl,e(f′).\Delta c_{l,e}^{(f)}=c_{l,e}^{(f)}-\frac{1}{K-1}\sum_{f^{\prime}\neq f}c_{l,e}^{(f^{\prime})}. (3)

We apply layer-wise z-score normalization across experts so that usage and coactivation advantages have comparable scales:

zscore⁡(xl,e(f))=xl,e(f)−μl(f)σl(f)+ϵ,\operatorname{zscore}(x_{l,e}^{(f)})=\frac{x_{l,e}^{(f)}-\mu_{l}^{(f)}}{\sigma_{l}^{(f)}+\epsilon}, (4)

where μl(f)\mu_{l}^{(f)} and σl(f)\sigma_{l}^{(f)} are the mean and standard deviation of xl,e(f)x_{l,e}^{(f)} over experts ee in layer ll for family ff, and ϵ\epsilon is a small constant for numerical stability.

After applying this normalization to both Δ​u\Delta u and Δ​c\Delta c, the soft preference score is

sl,e(f)=zscore⁡(Δ​ul,e(f))+zscore⁡(Δ​cl,e(f)),s_{l,e}^{(f)}=\operatorname{zscore}(\Delta u_{l,e}^{(f)})+\operatorname{zscore}(\Delta c_{l,e}^{(f)}), (5)

and a temperature-softmax converts this score into a soft task-family preference distribution:

pl,e(f)=exp⁡(sl,e(f)/τ)∑f′∈ℱexp⁡(sl,e(f′)/τ).p_{l,e}^{(f)}=\frac{\exp(s_{l,e}^{(f)}/\tau)}{\sum_{f^{\prime}\in\mathcal{F}}\exp(s_{l,e}^{(f^{\prime})}/\tau)}. (6)

The distribution pl,e(f)p_{l,e}^{(f)} preserves uncertainty for experts that are useful to multiple families. Crucially, TACG never converts pl,e(f)p_{l,e}^{(f)} into a rigid expert-to-family partition; it uses pl,e(f)p_{l,e}^{(f)} as a soft task signal that modulates the coactivation graph in the next step.

Task-modulated coactivation graph.

Pooled coactivation A¯l=1K​∑fAl(f)\bar{A}_{l}=\tfrac{1}{K}\sum_{f}A_{l}^{(f)} summarizes which experts are jointly accessed by a token, but it is task-agnostic: it treats coactivation edges across different families as equally valuable for locality. In multi-task serving, two experts that co-activate mainly on different families rarely meet on the same token, so placing them together wastes co-location capacity that would be better spent on same-family pairs. TACG therefore modulates the coactivation signal with the expert-to-family preference pl,e(f)p_{l,e}^{(f)} before grouping, so that the grouping step sees an affinity that favors expert pairs which both co-activate and tend to serve the same family.

Concretely, we stack the preferences into Pl∈ℝE×KP_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{E\times K} with (Pl)e,f=pl,e(f)(P_{l})_{e,f}=p_{l,e}^{(f)}, and form the same-family kernel

Altask=Pl​Pl⊤∈[0,1]E×E,Altask​(e,e′)=∑f∈ℱpl,e(f)​pl,e′(f),A_{l}^{\mathrm{task}}=P_{l}P_{l}^{\top}\in[0,1]^{E\times E},\qquad A_{l}^{\mathrm{task}}(e,e^{\prime})=\sum_{f\in\mathcal{F}}p_{l,e}^{(f)}\,p_{l,e^{\prime}}^{(f)}, (7)

which is the probability that two experts are drawn from the same family under independent family affiliations. With A^l=A¯l/max⁡A¯l\hat{A}_{l}=\bar{A}_{l}/\max\bar{A}_{l} normalized to [0,1][0,1], the task-modulated coactivation graph is

A~l=(1−α)​A^l+α⁡(Altask⊙A^l),\tilde{A}_{l}=(1-\alpha)\,\hat{A}_{l}+\alpha\,\bigl(A_{l}^{\mathrm{task}}\odot\hat{A}_{l}\bigr), (8)

where ⊙\odot denotes the Hadamard product and α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1] controls how strongly task structure reshapes coactivation. The multiplicative gate Altask⊙A^lA_{l}^{\mathrm{task}}\odot\hat{A}_{l} is the key design choice. It amplifies coactivation edges whose endpoints share a family and attenuates those that do not, without inventing new edges between experts that never co-activate. Thus pl,e(f)p_{l,e}^{(f)} enters grouping as a principled edge reweighting rather than a hard label.

Capacity-feasible expert grouping.

Given A~l\tilde{A}_{l}, we partition experts into MM exact-size groups {𝒮l,1,…,𝒮l,M}\{\mathcal{S}_{l,1},\ldots,\mathcal{S}_{l,M}\} by maximizing within-group affinity under per-GPU capacities:

max{𝒮l,m}∑m=1M∑e,e′∈𝒮l,mA~l(e,e′)s.t.|𝒮l,m|=Cm,⨆m=1M𝒮l,m={1,…,E}.\max_{\{\mathcal{S}_{l,m}\}}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\sum_{e,e^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}_{l,m}}\tilde{A}_{l}(e,e^{\prime})\quad\text{s.t.}\quad|\mathcal{S}_{l,m}|=C_{m},\ \ \bigsqcup_{m=1}^{M}\mathcal{S}_{l,m}=\{1,\ldots,E\}. (9)

This capacity-constrained graph partitioning problem is NP-hard, so we solve it with a two-stage spectral-then-repair procedure that is cheap to run offline and, empirically, very close to exhaustive search on the reweighted graph.

Stage 1: spectral clustering. We symmetrize A~l\tilde{A}_{l}, scale it to [0,1][0,1], and add a small diagonal jitter for numerical stability. Treating the result as a precomputed affinity, we apply normalized spectral clustering: we form the symmetric normalized Laplacian Lsym=I−D−1/2A~lD−1/2L_{\mathrm{sym}}=I-D^{-1/2}\tilde{A}_{l}D^{-1/2} with degree matrix DD, embed experts via its MM smallest eigenvectors, and run kk-means with k=Mk=M to obtain a soft partition {𝒮l,m0}\{\mathcal{S}_{l,m}^{0}\}. This step directly targets the relaxed within-group affinity objective and exposes the communities implied by the task-modulated graph, but it ignores the exact-size constraints |𝒮l,m|=Cm|\mathcal{S}_{l,m}|=C_{m}.

Stage 2: capacity repair. We enforce the per-GPU capacities with a local, affinity-guided repair that never re-runs spectral embedding. For every overfull group mm (with |𝒮l,m0|>Cm|\mathcal{S}_{l,m}^{0}|>C_{m}), we rank its members by their intra-group affinity ∑e′∈𝒮l,m0A~l​(e,e′)\sum_{e^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}_{l,m}^{0}}\tilde{A}_{l}(e,e^{\prime}) and keep the top-CmC_{m}; the remaining experts enter an overflow pool. Each overflow expert ee is then greedily inserted into the non-full group m⋆m^{\star} that yields the largest increase in within-group affinity, i.e.

m⋆(e)=argmaxm:|𝒮l,m|<Cm∑e′∈𝒮l,mA~l(e,e′).m^{\star}(e)=\arg\max_{m:\,|\mathcal{S}_{l,m}|<C_{m}}\,\sum_{e^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}_{l,m}}\tilde{A}_{l}(e,e^{\prime}). (10)

After this first pass, any residual size mismatches are resolved by a donor–receiver swap loop: for each still-underfull group 𝒮l,dst\mathcal{S}_{l,\mathrm{dst}}, we take the weakest member (lowest intra-group affinity) of an overfull donor group and move it to 𝒮l,dst\mathcal{S}_{l,\mathrm{dst}} only if the move improves the sum of within-group affinities. The loop terminates when all groups satisfy |𝒮l,m|=Cm|\mathcal{S}_{l,m}|=C_{m}, which is guaranteed within a bounded number of iterations since every accepted move strictly raises a monotone bounded objective.

In our experiments we fix α=0.25\alpha=0.25, which keeps communication as the dominant signal while gating out cross-family edges that hurt multi-task locality. The resulting assignment defines the primary placement gl,eprimaryg_{l,e}^{\mathrm{primary}}, which co-locates stable task-coherent expert communities and strictly generalizes task-agnostic grouping.

3.4 Generic Expert Shared Replication (GESR)

TACG delivers a stable and communication-efficient primary placement, but a small fraction of experts are generic: their coactivation profile is consistently central across families, so they are dispatched under every task and can become load hotspots. Replicating many experts would inflate memory cost and possibly create new hotspots, while a dedicated common-GPU would reintroduce exactly the cross-family traffic TACG eliminates. GESR addresses this risk with a minimal intervention on top of TACG: only a small set of generic experts receives secondary GPUs, and online selection is restricted to this candidate set, using TACG’s own coactivation structure as the compatibility criterion.

Identifying generic experts.

We identify generic experts using a score that favors global centrality and cross-family consistency while penalizing strong task-specific deviation. For expert ee at layer ll with pooled coactivation A¯l\bar{A}_{l},

rl,e=Centl,e⏟centrality+λ1​Consl,e⏟cross-family consistency−λ2​Specl,e⏟task-specific penalty,r_{l,e}=\underbrace{\mathrm{Cent}_{l,e}}_{\text{centrality}}+\lambda_{1}\underbrace{\mathrm{Cons}_{l,e}}_{\text{cross-family consistency}}-\lambda_{2}\underbrace{\mathrm{Spec}_{l,e}}_{\text{task-specific penalty}}, (11)

where Centl,e=∑e′A¯l​(e,e′)\mathrm{Cent}_{l,e}=\sum_{e^{\prime}}\bar{A}_{l}(e,e^{\prime}), Consl,e\mathrm{Cons}_{l,e} is the average cosine similarity between the expert’s family-specific coactivation profiles and their mean profile, and Specl,e\mathrm{Spec}_{l,e} is the maximum deviation from that mean profile across families.

For each layer, we select the top-scoring experts as generic experts. For each selected expert, we keep its TACG primary GPU and add a small number of secondary GPUs from structurally compatible non-primary GPUs, where compatibility is measured by coactivation affinity between the expert and the target card. This produces

𝒞l,e={gl,eprimary}∪{gl,e(1),gl,e(2),…}.\mathcal{C}_{l,e}=\{g_{l,e}^{\mathrm{primary}}\}\cup\{g_{l,e}^{(1)},g_{l,e}^{(2)},\ldots\}. (12)

For non-selected experts, the candidate set contains only the primary GPU. Because the secondary candidates are both sparse and coactivation-compatible with TACG, GESR preserves TACG’s communication structure while giving generic experts limited routing flexibility.

Locality- and load-aware serving.

At inference time, the MoE router output is left unchanged; the serving system only chooses which candidate GPU serves a selected expert. Let ℛ\mathcal{R} be the set of GPUs already accessed by the current token, aa the token’s anchor GPU, and f⁡(x)f(x) its task family. We maintain an exponentially decayed recent load LmL_{m} for each GPU and define

L¯=1M​∑mLm.\bar{L}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m}L_{m}. (13)

For a generic expert, candidates whose recent load is within a tolerance θ\theta form the feasible set

𝒞l,efeas={m∈𝒞l,e:Lm≤(1+θ)​L¯}.\mathcal{C}_{l,e}^{\mathrm{feas}}=\{m\in\mathcal{C}_{l,e}:L_{m}\leq(1+\theta)\bar{L}\}. (14)

If the feasible set is empty, we fall back to the full candidate set 𝒞l,e\mathcal{C}_{l,e}. After dispatch, the recent load is updated as

Lm←ρ​Lm+Δm,L_{m}\leftarrow\rho L_{m}+\Delta_{m}, (15)

where ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1) is the decay factor and Δm\Delta_{m} is the dispatch increment contributed by the current token.

4 Experiments

In this section, we conduct experiments to address the following research questions:

  • •

    RQ1: Does TACG + GESR reduce communication more than strong placement baselines while preserving load balance?

  • •

    RQ2: Does the advantage of TACG+GESR reflect genuine task-aware decoupling rather than a calibration artifact, and does it persist under skewed, unseen task distributions where same-family experts remain co-located and GESR absorbs residual hotspots?

  • •

    RQ3: How much does each design choice—task-modulated coactivation, task-family preference, generic-expert replication, and the load guard—contribute to the final performance?

  • •

    RQ4: Is GESR’s specificity-penalized replica-selection criterion the right one, and does it remain effective under task skew?

4.1 Experimental Setup

Following Section 3.3, we partition multi-task traffic into K=4K{=}4 task families: code, query, math, and complex_reasoning, each populated from widely used open datasets (full list in Appendix D). Calibration traces feed per-family usage and coactivation statistics, but are never reused as evaluation streams. We deploy each model on a 1616-GPU expert-parallel target (M=16M{=}16), allocating 44 GPUs to each of the four task families. Per-GPU capacities saturate the per-family budgets (∑mCf,m=Bf\sum_{m}C_{f,m}{=}B_{f} and ∑fBf=E\sum_{f}B_{f}{=}E). All methods are evaluated under identical capacity constraints.

Models.

We evaluate our framework on three representative open-source MoE language models that span two architectural styles and three vendors: DeepSeek-MoE-16B [19], Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B [27], and Moonlight-16B-A3B [28].

Baselines.

We compare against a set of strong recent placement baselines: (i) Baseline, the model’s default expert placement; (ii) Frequency and (iii) Coactivation, two canonical statistical placements; (iv) Sem.P. [6], a semantic-parallelism placement; (v) ExFlow [12]; (vi) MoETuner [14]; and (vii) C2R [13]. All baselines use the same experimental setup. Further models and baselines details are provided in Appendix E, G.

Metrics.

We report four system-level metrics that jointly characterize communication efficiency and load balance: Comm, Comm. Red., Jain and MaxVio. A detailed explanation is provided in Appendix H.

4.2 Main Comparison with Placement Baselines (RQ1)

Table 1 summarizes the primary comparison on the canonical multi-task workload across all three MoE models. Our framework (TACG + GESR) achieves the highest communication reduction on every model and on the cross-model average, while simultaneously attaining a load-balance profile that is strictly superior to every non-trivial baseline.

Obs. 1: Task-aware placement yields the largest communication reduction by a substantial margin.

Our method reduces per-token communication by 31.39% on average, 12.58% better than the strongest prior (ExFlow, 18.81%) and 14.88%–23.51% better than the other five baselines. The reduction is consistent across models (30.47%–32.28%), confirming the gain stems from the placement principle rather than any specific router or expert count.

Obs. 2: The communication reduction is not obtained at the cost of load balance.

Prior methods often sacrifice load balance. e.g., Frequency and ExFlow cause MaxVio >> 1 and Jain << 0.9 on Moonlight, while Coactivation, Semantic Parallelism, and C2R inflate MaxVio on multiple models. In contrast, our framework achieves the best MaxVio on every model (0.0472–0.1141); Table 1) and an average Jain of 0.9975, matching the Baseline’s fairness while cutting communication by 1/3. It also uniformly outperforms MoETuner, the most load-balance-oriented prior.

4.3 Is the Gain a Genuine Task-Aware Decoupling? (RQ2)

Table 1 establishes a quantitative advantage of our framework on the canonical mix, but does not, by itself, adjudicate its underlying cause. A possible alternative explanation is that TACG has overfit to a one-shot statistic of the calibration mix, rather than recovering task-conditioned structure that generalizes beyond it. A genuine task-aware decoupling should therefore remain effective when the online task distribution deviates substantially from the calibration distribution. We test this hypothesis by holding the placement fixed at its canonical calibration and evaluating it under a sweep of workload-skew regimes to which it has not been fitted (Figure 3, DeepSeek-MoE-16B).

Obs. 3: Communication advantage persists under severe task-distribution skew.

Since the two placements in Figure 3 differ only in task-family preference, the gap between Ours and Ours w/o task preference isolates task-awareness. Under OOD single-task traffic, removing task-awareness causes MaxVioGlobal to surge—2.037 vs. 0.294 on Code (≈7×\approx 7\times), and ≈2×\approx 2\times on Math and Query (Fig. 3(b))—while Ours remains low. Task-aware alignment lets a single-task burst spread across the expert family’s GPU set; a task-agnostic graph instead packs heterogeneous families onto the same devices and collapses the burst into a hotspot. As Fig. 3(a) shows, Ours achieves a markedly steadier reduction rate with far lower variance across workloads, whereas the task-agnostic variant suffers from large swings. Such stable, low-variance gains confirm that task-aware placement strictly advances the communication–balance frontier, not a one-shot calibration artifact.

4.4 Ablation and Design-Choice Analysis (RQ3)

We next decompose the contribution of each building block of our framework. Cross-model averages are reported in Table 2.

Obs. 4: Task-conditioned coactivation dominates; both signals are necessary only jointly.

Replacing the task-modulated coactivation graph with a uniform affinity (w/o coactivation) drops the communication reduction from 31.39%31.39\% to 16.51%16.51\%; disabling task-family preference (α=0\alpha{=}0) reduces it by 9.98%9.98\% and triples MaxVio (0.0736→0.24160.0736{\to}0.2416). Only their joint interaction recovers the full +31.39%+31.39\% gain, confirming that task-conditioning is indispensable and the two signals are complementary.

Obs. 5: GESR acts as a targeted load-balance safeguard.

Removing GESR keeps communication gains high (+24.23%+24.23\%) but nearly quadruples MaxVio (0.0736→\to0.2763) and pushes the Jain index below 0.99. With GESR but θ\theta disabled, reduction surges to +35.87%+35.87\% at the cost of MaxVio 0.1422. Only the full TACG + GESR with active θ\theta reaches the communication–balance frontier, thereby separating the framework into a primary communication-reduction module (task-conditioned coactivation) and a load-balance safeguard (GESR with θ\theta), as designed in Section 4.1.

4.5 GESR Replica-Selection Design under Severe Task Skew (RQ4)

Obs. 5 shows that removing GESR inflates MaxVio, but does not yet justify its specific form—centrality plus cross-family consistency reward and family-specificity penalty (Section 3.4). We therefore isolate the replica-selection criterion and ask whether GESR’s specificity-aware design pays off under task-distribution drift. We reuse the extreme single-family skew setup of Section 4.3: TACG’s primary placement is held fixed at its canonical calibration, and we vary only the replica scorer across NoRep, Freq-TopK, Hot, Coact-Cent (centrality-only, a stripped-down GESR), Random, and Gesr.

Obs. 6: GESR’s specificity-aware scorer improves hotspot robustness at no communication cost.

Gesr attains the lowest MaxVio on unseen families (Figure 4(a)), reducing hotspots by 2.1%2.1\% over the best coactivation-only baseline and by 15​–​17%15\text{--}17\% over frequency/hot baselines, while matching Coact-Cent on communication (Figure 4(b)). The gain is therefore a strict improvement.

5 Limitations and Future Work

Our work focuses on a static offline placement and leaves three directions open. (i) Dynamic regrouping: we recompute placement only on substantial workload drift; online regrouping within a request window could further close the gap to oracle placement under rapid shifts. (ii) Memory co-design: we enforce a hard per-GPU memory bound; integrating expert prefetching, caching, and offloading with our placement is a promising orthogonal direction for additional latency gains. (iii) Specialized experts: our evaluation targets general-purpose MoE models; we expect larger improvements from TACG and GESR on models with explicitly specialized experts (e.g., domain- or modality-partitioned), and we leave a systematic study for future work.

6 Conclusion

We show that expert coactivation in multi-task MoE serving is strongly task-conditioned and should directly drive placement. TACG exploits this signal to build a capacity-feasible primary placement, and GESR replicates a few generic experts with load-aware online selection to protect locality under drift. Across three MoE models, the combined framework cuts per-token communication by 31.39%31.39\% while keeping Jain 0.99750.9975 and MaxVio 0.07360.0736 (Tables 1, 2).

Appendix A Sensitivity to the Calibration Token Budget

A practical concern for any calibration-based placement method is how many calibration tokens it actually needs. To answer this we run the full placement pipeline on DeepSeek-MoE-16B while sweeping the per-sample calibration cap from 11 token to 20482048 tokens (with one calibration sample per family); under this protocol the resulting calibration corpus grows from 99 tokens at tokcap=1=1 to ∼2\sim\!2k tokens at tokcap=2048=2048. Six baselines and Ours are recalibrated on each budget and evaluated on the held-out test stream. All other settings (top-kk, M=16M=16, per-family GPU groups) follow the main protocol.

Obs. A1: TACG + GESR converges with hundreds, not millions, of calibration tokens.

With as few as 3636 calibration tokens Ours already exceeds +18%+18\% Comm. Red. on DeepSeek-MoE-16B, surpassing the full-budget Coactivation/Frequency/MoETuner/C2R baselines. The curve enters a plateau around 128128–256256 tokens (Figure 5); doubling the budget further from ∼600\sim\!600 to ∼2,000\sim\!2{,}000 tokens improves Comm. Red. by less than 0.70.7 points. We attribute this fast convergence to the fact that TACG only needs to estimate per-family relative coactivation orderings, not full distributions, and GESR’s score Cent+λ1​Cons−λ2​Spec\mathrm{Cent}+\lambda_{1}\mathrm{Cons}-\lambda_{2}\mathrm{Spec} depends only on aggregate centrality and per-family means, both of which stabilize quickly.

Appendix B Hyperparameter Sensitivity

Our framework exposes three hyperparameters that warrant a sensitivity study: (i) the TACG task-preference strength α\alpha that trades off pure co-activation locality against task-modulated grouping (Section 3.3); (ii) the GESR scoring coefficients (λ1,λ2)(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}) that trade off cross-family consistency against family-specific deviation (Section 3.4); and (iii) the load-guard slack θ\theta that bounds the secondary-card admission rule at serving time (Section 3.4). Each sweep varies one hyperparameter while holding all others at their canonical values (α=0.25\alpha=0.25, λ1=0\lambda_{1}{=}0, λ2=0\lambda_{2}{=}0, θ=0.15\theta=0.15, replica budget nrep=8n_{\mathrm{rep}}{=}8, ksec=2k_{\mathrm{sec}}{=}2, decay ρ=0.995\rho{=}0.995). Unless noted, every reported value is the cross-model average over DeepSeek-MoE-16B, Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B, and Moonlight-16B-A3B.

B.1 Task-Preference Strength α\alpha

The task-preference strength α\alpha interpolates between task-agnostic co-activation grouping and TACG’s task-modulated objective (Section 3.3). At α=0\alpha{=}0 every expert is pinned to its physical home family, which recovers the task-agnostic family partition (equivalent to Ours w/o task preference in the ablation table). We sweep α∈{0,0.05,0.10,0.25,0.50,0.75,1.00}\alpha\!\in\!\{0,0.05,0.10,0.25,0.50,0.75,1.00\}.

Obs. A1: Task modulation saturates at α⋆\alpha^{\star}, and the canonical choice sits at the knee.

Table 3 shows a clear two-regime behaviour. In the family-pinned regime (α<α⋆\alpha<\alpha^{\star}), Comm. Red. is stuck around +21+21–22%22\% and MaxVio is an order of magnitude worse (0.220.22–0.250.25) because pinning experts to their physical home ignores the actual task-conditioned co-activation structure. Once α\alpha crosses the pivot, every metric improves abruptly: Comm. Red. jumps to +31.85%+31.85\% (+10+10%), MaxVio drops to 0.0740.074 (−0.18-0.18), and Jain rises to 0.9980.998. Further increasing α\alpha up to 1.01.0 changes Comm. Red. by at most 0.70.7% and MaxVio by ≤0.013\leq 0.013, indicating that once TACG is activated the result is insensitive to the exact weight. We use α=0.25\alpha{=}0.25 in the main paper because it is the smallest value that realises the full task-modulated benefit; the same conclusion holds on each individual backbone (DeepSeek: +32.82%+32.82\%, Moonlight: +30.93%+30.93\%, Qwen: +31.79%+31.79\% at α=0.25\alpha{=}0.25).

B.2 GESR Scoring Coefficients (λ1,λ2)(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2})

GESR scores generic experts by rl,e=Centl,e+λ1​Consl,e−λ2​Specl,er_{l,e}=\mathrm{Cent}_{l,e}+\lambda_{1}\,\mathrm{Cons}_{l,e}-\lambda_{2}\,\mathrm{Spec}_{l,e}, where λ1\lambda_{1} rewards cross-family consistency and λ2\lambda_{2} penalizes family-specific deviation. We sweep λ1∈{0,0.1,0.25,0.5,1.0,2.0}\lambda_{1}\in\{0,0.1,0.25,0.5,1.0,2.0\} and λ2∈{0,0.05,0.1,0.25,0.5,1.0}\lambda_{2}\in\{0,0.05,0.1,0.25,0.5,1.0\}, holding the replica budget fixed at nrep=8n_{\mathrm{rep}}{=}8, ksec=2k_{\mathrm{sec}}{=}2. The extra-memory cost is identical across all cells (+25.6%+25.6\% on average), so we omit it.

Obs. A2: Centrality is the dominant signal; both regularizers are mild and self-limiting.

Across the entire grid (Figure 6), Comm. Red. stays within a narrow band of 28.5%28.5\%–30.8%30.8\% and MaxVio within 0.0880.088–0.1890.189. Increasing λ2\lambda_{2} aggressively (column λ2=1.0\lambda_{2}{=}1.0) is the single most damaging move: it suppresses generic experts that happen to skew toward one family, which removes useful replicas and therefore both lowers Comm. Red. (−1-1 to −2-2 pp) and raises MaxVio (up to 0.1890.189). Increasing λ1\lambda_{1} aggressively (row λ1=2\lambda_{1}{=}2) similarly degrades Comm. Red. by ∼1\sim\!1 pp by promoting experts whose cross-family consistency is high but whose centrality is moderate. Both regularizers are best kept small: any (λ1,λ2)∈[0,0.5]×[0,0.25](\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2})\in[0,0.5]\times[0,0.25] is within 0.40.4 pp of the optimum, justifying the canonical choice (0,0)(0,0) that uses pure centrality.

B.3 Load-Guard Slack θ\theta

The serving-time load guard restricts secondary-card admission to candidates whose recent load is at most (1+θ)​L¯(1+\theta)\bar{L}, where L¯\bar{L} is the recent per-GPU mean (Section 3.4). Setting θ→∞\theta\!\to\!\infty disables the guard (equivalent to Ours w/o load guard in the ablation table); setting θ=0\theta\!=\!0 admits only below-average GPUs and corresponds to the strictest balance regime.

Obs. A3: The communication–balance trade-off is monotone and well-behaved in θ\theta.

Comm. Red. rises monotonically from +28.1%+28.1\% at θ=0\theta{=}0 to +36.1%+36.1\% at θ→∞\theta{\to}\infty, while MaxVio grows in the opposite direction from 0.0660.066 to 0.1610.161 (Figure 7). The frontier is therefore a single one-dimensional curve, and choosing θ\theta amounts to choosing an operating point on it. We use θ=0.15\theta=0.15 in the main paper because it is the smallest slack that captures most of the available communication gain (+31.85%+31.85\%, only ∼4\sim\!4 pp below the unguarded extreme) while keeping MaxVio at 0.0740.074, well below the 0.100.10 threshold at which Jain starts to drop noticeably. Importantly, the rerouting rate stays close to 50%50\% across the entire sweep: the load guard reshapes which secondary card is selected rather than throttling secondary use.

Appendix C Per-Token Communication Trace Analysis

To confirm visually that the Comm. Red. gains in Section 4.2 stem from task-aware colocation rather than incidental graph structure, we compare per-token dispatch traces of Ours (TACG + GESR) against the strongest pooled-coactivation baseline (Coactivation) on DeepSeek-MoE-16B. Each token traverses 2727 MoE layers; under a fixed expert-to-GPU grouping, every layer dispatches its top-kk experts to one or more GPUs, which we record as: (i) cross-group dispatch count per token, ∑lmax⁡(0,|cardsl|−1)\sum_{l}\max(0,|\mathrm{cards}_{l}|-1), equal to the cross_group_comm_count of the main table; (ii) cross-family layers per token, the number of layers whose dispatch set spans more than one family; and (iii) home-family dispatch-mass concentration, the fraction of dispatch mass that stays within the four GPUs of the token’s home family (25%25\% uniform baseline). All three are measured per task family on the held-out test stream.

Obs. A4: Ours cuts per-layer cross-group hops uniformly across all four families.

Ours reduces the per-token cross-group hop count by 1515–19%19\% on every family (Table 4), an improvement that closely tracks the headline Comm. Red. in Section 4.2 and confirms that the system-level gains compose directly from per-layer dispatch reductions rather than from better load balance alone.

Appendix D Additional Experimental Setup

Calibration corpora.

For each task family in Section 4.1 we draw calibration tokens from a small set of widely used open datasets: mbpp, humaneval, apps-intro for code; sql, spider for query; gsm8k, numina-math for math; and bbh, legal for complex_reasoning. Calibration tokens feed only the per-family usage and coactivation statistics, and are never reused as an evaluation stream. The complete introduction of each dataset is in Appendix F.

Per-GPU expert capacities.

The four per-family GPU groups are kept symmetric: each MoE layer is deployed on M=16M{=}16 GPUs partitioned into four groups of four GPUs, one per task family. Per-GPU capacities saturate the per-family expert budgets exactly: {4,4,4,4}\{4,4,4,4\} for DeepSeek-MoE-16B and Moonlight-16B-A3B (both E=64E{=}64 routed experts per layer), and {4,4,4,3}\{4,4,4,3\} for Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B (E=60E{=}60).

Stress-workload suite for the skew sweep.

The skew study in Section 4.3 sweeps 1313 online workloads that all reuse the same calibrated placement: one balanced reference; eight single-family-heavy streams (four families ×\times two skew shares {0.6,0.8}\{0.6,0.8\}); two temporal phase-shift workloads that alternate the dominant family over time; and two bursty workloads that inject a 15%15\% burst of math or complex_reasoning tokens on top of the balanced base. Only the online token stream changes across workloads; the deployed expert–GPU assignment is held fixed.

Appendix E Models

We evaluate three representative open-source sparse MoE backbones whose router structure and expert granularity span the design space we wish to stress (Table 5).

DeepSeek-MoE-16B [19] adopts fine-grained expert segmentation, in which each FFN is split into a larger number of smaller experts to enrich the per-token expert combination, and shared-expert isolation, in which two always-on experts capture common knowledge so that the routed experts can specialize. The model is trained from scratch on 22T Chinese–English tokens. Each MoE layer activates the two shared experts plus the top-66 of 6464 routed experts.

Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B [27] is a 14.314.3B-parameter MoE upcycled from the dense Qwen-1.8B backbone rather than trained from scratch, reportedly using ∼25%\sim\!25\% of the training resources of Qwen1.5-7B at comparable quality. Each MoE layer routes each token to top-44 of 6060 routed experts on top of 44 always-on shared experts.

Moonlight-16B-A3B [28] follows a DeepSeek-V3-style sparse architecture and is trained on 5.75.7T tokens with the Muon optimizer. The first decoder layer is dense; each of the remaining 2626 MoE layers activates two shared experts plus top-66 of 6464 routed experts.

Appendix F Tasks and Datasets

MBPP [29] contains crowd-sourced Python programming problems paired with reference solutions and unit tests. It probes natural-language-to-code generation and basic program synthesis ability.

HumanEval [30] is also a Python code generation benchmark. Each problem usually contains a function signature, a natural language docstring, and hidden unit tests. It evaluates whether the model can generate functionally correct Python functions.

APPS-Intro [31] is the introductory subset of the APPS programming benchmark. Compared with HumanEval, APPS problems are usually closer to full programming contest-style questions, where the model needs to understand the problem statement and generate a complete program that passes input-output tests. Together, these datasets represent the Code family.

Spider [32] is a cross-domain text-to-SQL benchmark whose multi-table schemas and nested queries probe structured-query generation. It evaluates whether a model can map a natural language question and a database schema to an executable SQL query.

SQL [33] refers to a general text-to-SQL dataset used for calibration in this work. It contains natural language questions, database contexts or schemas, and corresponding SQL queries. It is used to capture routing patterns related to structured query generation. Together, Spider and SQL represent the Query family.

GSM8K [34] comprises human-written grade-school math word problems whose solutions require multi-step arithmetic reasoning. It mainly tests whether a model can extract quantitative relations from natural language and solve them through step-by-step calculation.

Numina-Math [35] is a larger mathematical reasoning dataset that covers a wider range of math problems and solution styles. It is useful for collecting calibration traces that reflect more diverse mathematical reasoning patterns. Together, GSM8K and Numina-Math represent the Math family.

Legal [36] contains long, terminology-dense passages drawn from statutes, contracts, and case law, and probes long-context professional reasoning.

BBH [37], or BIG-Bench Hard, is a collection of challenging reasoning tasks selected from BIG-Bench. It covers tasks that require multi-step reasoning, symbolic manipulation, logical inference, and complex language understanding. We use BBH together with Legal to represent the Complex Reasoning family, since both datasets require more complex reasoning paths than standard generation tasks. The four task families jointly cover code generation, structured generation, numeric reasoning, and long-context or complex professional reasoning, four regimes whose expert activation patterns are expected to differ substantially.

Appendix G Baseline Methods

ExFlow [8] accelerates pre-trained MoE inference by exploiting the implicit inter-layer expert affinity: experts that frequently fire together across consecutive layers are colocated, and a context-coherent expert-parallel scheme keeps token context on its current GPU so that one All-to-All per layer is sufficient. ExFlow optimizes only placement and requires no fine-tuning.

Semantic Parallelism [6] performs offline token-to-expert profiling, clusters experts that are activated by semantically similar tokens onto the same device, and then schedules online traffic accordingly: request-level scheduling under attention-DP and token-level reshuffling under attention-TP, so that tokens are moved in advance toward the devices that are more likely to host their target experts.

MoETuner [14] formulates expert placement as an integer linear program over a profiled cross-layer token routing graph. The objective jointly minimizes per-GPU parameter cost, dispatch load imbalance, cross-GPU communication volume, and tail latency, exploiting the empirical observation that a token routed to a particular expert at one layer is likely routed to a small subset of experts at the next.

C2R [13] (Collaboration-Constrained Routing) builds a per-layer expert-collaboration matrix from profiling, and at routing time first picks the top-11 expert and then restricts the remaining K−1K{-}1 slots to the experts most often coactivated with it. Coactivated experts are colocated, so that one All-to-All hop suffices to deliver a token to its full expert subset on the local GPU.

Appendix H Metric Definitions

System-level metrics.

We use four system-level metrics that jointly characterize the communication–load-balance trade-off of an MoE deployment.

Comm is the per-token cross-GPU dispatch volume during MoE inference: every layer in which a token’s selected experts span more than one GPU contributes one cross-GPU hop. Lower is better.

Comm. Red. (Communication Reduction) reports the relative drop in Comm against the vendor default placement baseline,

Comm.Red.=CommBaseline−CommMethodCommBaseline×100%.\mathrm{Comm.\ Red.}=\frac{\mathrm{Comm}_{\mathrm{Baseline}}-\mathrm{Comm}_{\mathrm{Method}}}{\mathrm{Comm}_{\mathrm{Baseline}}}\times 100\%. (16)

Higher is better.

Jain is Jain’s Fairness Index over the per-GPU dispatch loads {Lm}m=1M\{L_{m}\}_{m=1}^{M},

Jain=(∑m=1MLm)2M​∑m=1MLm2∈(0,1],\mathrm{Jain}=\frac{\left(\sum_{m=1}^{M}L_{m}\right)^{2}}{M\sum_{m=1}^{M}L_{m}^{2}}\in(0,1], (17)

which is a global measure of load uniformity (closer to 11 is better).

MaxVio (Maximum Load Violation) measures the relative overload of the worst-case GPU,

MaxVio=Lmax−L¯L¯,L¯=1M​∑mLm.\mathrm{MaxVio}=\frac{L_{\max}-\bar{L}}{\bar{L}},\qquad\bar{L}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m}L_{m}. (18)

Unlike Jain, MaxVio is dominated by the most overloaded device and therefore tracks the bottleneck risk of the system. Lower is better.

Δ\DeltaComm reports the additive change in Comm. Red. of an ablation variant relative to the full method. A negative value means removing the module hurts; a positive value alone is not a sign of improvement, since the variant may have traded load balance for raw communication reduction (e.g., w/o load guard reaches +35.87%+35.87\% Comm. Red. but inflates MaxVio to 0.14220.1422, vs. the full method at +31.39%+31.39\% and 0.07360.0736).

Auxiliary motivation metrics.

To substantiate the claim that expert coactivation is task-conditioned (Section 1), we report three auxiliary diagnostics on calibration tokens. Per-task expert activation is the per-expert activation probability under each task family, used to visualize task-specific expert preferences. The activation Frobenius distance between two task families is the Frobenius norm ‖Pi−Pj‖F\|P_{i}-P_{j}\|_{F} of the difference between their expert-activation distributions; larger values indicate that the two families exercise different experts. The top-6464 pair Jaccard overlap measures the Jaccard similarity between the sets of top-6464 most frequently coactivated expert pairs of two task families; lower values indicate that the two families exercise different expert–expert collaboration structures. Together these diagnostics show that a globally pooled affinity graph hides task-specific coactivation patterns and motivates the task-aware grouping in Section 3.3.

NeurIPS Paper Checklist

The checklist is designed to encourage best practices for responsible machine learning research, addressing issues of reproducibility, transparency, research ethics, and societal impact. Do not remove the checklist: The papers not including the checklist will be desk rejected. The checklist should follow the references and follow the (optional) supplemental material. The checklist does NOT count towards the page limit.

Please read the checklist guidelines carefully for information on how to answer these questions. For each question in the checklist:

  • •

    You should answer [Yes] , [No] , or [N/A] .

  • •

    [N/A] means either that the question is Not Applicable for that particular paper or the relevant information is Not Available.

  • •

    Please provide a short (1–2 sentence) justification right after your answer (even for [N/A] ).

The checklist answers are an integral part of your paper submission. They are visible to the reviewers, area chairs, senior area chairs, and ethics reviewers. You will also be asked to include it (after eventual revisions) with the final version of your paper, and its final version will be published with the paper.

The reviewers of your paper will be asked to use the checklist as one of the factors in their evaluation. While [Yes] is generally preferable to [No] , it is perfectly acceptable to answer [No] provided a proper justification is given (e.g., error bars are not reported because it would be too computationally expensive” or “we were unable to find the license for the dataset we used”). In general, answering [No] or [N/A] is not grounds for rejection. While the questions are phrased in a binary way, we acknowledge that the true answer is often more nuanced, so please just use your best judgment and write a justification to elaborate. All supporting evidence can appear either in the main paper or the supplemental material, provided in appendix. If you answer [Yes] to a question, in the justification please point to the section(s) where related material for the question can be found.

    • •

      The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings.

    • •

      It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper.

    • •

The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon.

    • •

      The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size.

In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed.
